stimuli.title: The Dinghy
stimuli.text:
The dinghy had been upside down under the jacaranda for three summers, and in that time it had become part of the yard, like the clothesline or the cracked birdbath. Nobody looked at it any more. So when Nell dragged it into the sun on the first Saturday of the holidays and announced that she was going to sail it, Jai laughed before he could stop himself.

"It's got a hole in it," he said. "A big one. Possums live in it. You'll never finish it."

"Lived," said Nell, flipping it over with a grunt. A grey blur shot out from under the bow and vanished into the hedge. "Past tense."

She worked on it every afternoon. Jai told himself he wasn't watching, but from his bedroom window he could see her bent over the hull, sanding the timber in long, patient strokes until the old blue paint gave way to wood the colour of honey. She didn't ask for help. That was the annoying part. Nell had always asked Jai for help: with her maths, with her shoelaces when she was little, with the lid of the peanut butter jar. Now she had a library book about boat repair propped open on a brick, and she read it the way other people read adventure stories.

On the ninth day Jai wandered out with two glasses of cordial and set one down beside her without a word.

"Thanks," she said, not looking up. Then: "Can you hold this?"

It was a strip of fibreglass cloth, sticky and stiff. He held it while she smoothed resin over the hole, and the smell made his eyes water. Neither of them mentioned that he had said she'd never finish.

When the patch had set, Nell ran her palm across it, slowly, the way you might stroke a sleeping dog.

"Dad says if it floats, we can take it down to the lake next weekend," she said. "Both of us. It needs someone to bail."

"Bail?" said Jai. "So it still leaks?"

Nell grinned at him, and for a moment she looked exactly like the little sister who used to beg him to open the peanut butter.

"Only a bit," she said. "That's what you're for."

stimuli.title: First Rain
stimuli.text:
For eleven months the paddocks lay
like an old dog's coat, worn thin and grey;
the dam was a mirror cracked in two,
the sky an empty, endless blue.

Dad checked the gauge each morning, then
he tapped the glass and checked again,
as if a stare could make it fill.
The windmill turned. The tank stayed still.

Then Tuesday, late, the air went tight.
The cockatoos flew off in fright.
A smell of dust and pennies, cold,
came first, before the thunder rolled.

And then it fell. It fell and fell,
on roof and trough and rusted well;
it drummed the shed, it filled each rut,
it found the door we'd never shut.

And Dad stood out there in his hat,
not running in, not minding that
his shirt was soaked right through. He stayed,
face up, the way some people pray.

stimuli.title: Shade Is Not a Luxury
stimuli.text:
On a hot January afternoon, walk down a street with no trees and then walk down one lined with old figs or gums. You will not need a thermometer to feel the difference, but scientists have measured it anyway. In studies of hot suburbs, footpaths in full sun have reached surface temperatures more than 20 degrees higher than footpaths in the shade of a large tree.

That matters because our cities are getting hotter. Roads, roofs and car parks soak up the sun's heat during the day and release it slowly at night, so some suburbs never really cool down. Scientists call this the "urban heat island" effect. It is hardest on the people with the least protection: older residents, babies, and anyone who cannot afford to run air conditioning all summer.

Trees are the cheapest air conditioners we have. A mature tree shades the ground, and it also releases water through its leaves, which cools the air around it. It does all this without a power bill. Yet in many new housing estates, trees are the first thing to go. Blocks are smaller, houses fill almost every square metre, and the footpaths are left bare.

Some councils are fighting back. They have set targets to cover a larger share of their suburbs with tree canopy, and they plant thousands of saplings every winter. Residents can help too, by asking for a street tree outside their home, or by watering the young ones through their first two summers, when they are most likely to die.

Of course, trees are not perfect neighbours. Their roots can lift footpaths, and their leaves block gutters. These are real problems, but they are small ones, and they can be managed by choosing the right species for the right place.

The truth is simple: a suburb without shade is a suburb designed for cars, not people. If we want our neighbourhoods to stay liveable as summers grow longer, we need to stop treating trees as decoration and start treating them as infrastructure, as necessary as water pipes and power lines.

stimuli.title: How the Platypus Hunts
stimuli.text:
The platypus is one of the strangest animals on Earth, and its oddest feature may be the way it finds its food. It hunts on the bottom of creeks and rivers, mostly at night, in water that is often muddy. **[Gap 1]** For a long time, scientists could not understand how it caught anything at all.

The answer lies in its bill. Although it looks like a duck's, the bill is soft and leathery, and it is packed with tens of thousands of tiny sensors. **[Gap 2]** Every time a shrimp flicks its tail or a worm tightens its muscles, it gives off a faint electric signal. The platypus picks up these signals as it sweeps its bill from side to side across the riverbed.

Other sensors in the bill respond to touch and to tiny ripples in the water. **[Gap 3]** Scientists think the platypus may compare the two, in a similar way to how we can judge the distance of a storm by counting the seconds between the lightning and the thunder.

Hunting this way takes a great deal of energy. **[Gap 4]** That would be like a 40-kilogram child eating eight kilograms of food every day. To find so much, a platypus may spend ten to twelve hours a day foraging. Most dives last less than a minute, so it may dive hundreds of times in a single night.

The platypus does not eat underwater. Instead, it stores its catch in pouches in its cheeks, along with a little gravel from the riverbed. **[Gap 5]** Then it floats on the surface, grinding the meal between hard pads in its bill, since adult platypuses have no teeth.

The platypus is native only to eastern Australia, from north Queensland to Tasmania. Today it faces new threats. Dams change the flow of rivers, droughts dry up the deep pools where it shelters, and some kinds of fishing traps can drown it. **[Gap 6]** In several rivers, volunteers now help scientists survey platypuses each year to find out whether their numbers are falling.

stimuli.title: Lost
stimuli.text:
**Extract A**

Saturday 14 March

Dad's famous shortcut added two hours to our walk. The track on his map went straight down to the waterfall. The track on the ground had other ideas: it wandered off along a ridge, crossed a creek twice and then simply stopped in a patch of lantana. We had to turn around and go back the long way. My little brother Sam had eaten all the scroggin by eleven o'clock, so lunch was one apple, shared four ways. We reached the falls at three, sunburnt and cranky, and Mum made Dad promise to follow the signs next time. I'm writing this in the back seat on the drive home, and my legs feel like cooked spaghetti.

**Extract B**

If you become lost in the bush, the most important thing to do is stop. Walking on in search of the track often leads people further away from it, and it makes the job of rescuers harder, because they begin by searching along the route you were expected to take. Find shelter nearby, stay warm and drink water if you have it. Three short blasts on a whistle are widely recognised as a call for help. Bright clothing, or anything shiny laid out in an open space, will make you easier to spot from a helicopter. Before any walk, always tell someone where you are going and when you expect to return.

**Extract C**

I was six when I lost my grandmother at the Saturday markets. One moment my hand was in hers; the next, I was holding a fold of a stranger's skirt. I remember a forest of legs, the smell of fried dough and the shouting of the fruit sellers. I did not cry. I was too busy being furious that she had let go. When she finally found me beside the fish stall, she was the one in tears, and she held me so tightly that my ribs hurt. For years I told that story as proof of how brave I was. Now that I have children of my own, I think it is really a story about her.

**Extract D**

The fog rolled in off the sea so quickly that by the time Ari reached the top of the dune, the car park had vanished. So had the path, the fence and the lifeguard tower. Everything was the same soft grey. She stood very still and listened. The waves were booming somewhere on her left, which meant the road had to be on her right. Keeping the roar of the surf behind her shoulder, she walked slowly, counting her steps, until her feet found bitumen and two yellow headlights loomed out of the whiteness. Her uncle wound down the window. "Took your time," he said, and handed her the thermos.

stimuli.title: The Night Sky
stimuli.text:
**Text 1**

*Out Past the Last Streetlight*

Out past the last streetlight, where the bitumen ends
and the gravel crunches under our thongs,
Gran switches off the torch and says, "Now look."

And there it is: the whole spilled bag of it,
the Milky Way like flour across a dark bench,
the Southern Cross tipped on its side,
so many stars that the black between them
seems to be the thing that's rare.

At home in the city, I can name
the four stars I can see from my window.
I thought that was the sky.

Gran says her grandmother read this sky
like a calendar, and knew when to plant
by which stars rose before the sun.
I stand there with my neck aching,
trying to read one word of it.

**Text 2**

*Losing the Dark*

More than 80 per cent of the world's people now live under skies brightened by artificial light, and more than a third of humanity can no longer see the Milky Way from home. Light pollution is not only a loss for stargazers. Newly hatched sea turtles head for the brightest horizon, which should be the moonlit sea; near towns, many crawl towards streetlights instead. Migrating birds can become confused by brightly lit buildings and circle them until they are exhausted.

The good news is that light pollution is one of the easiest kinds of pollution to fix. Shielded lights that point downwards, warmer bulbs, and switching off lights that no one needs can bring back much of the dark almost overnight. Some towns have already made these changes, and they now attract visitors who come simply to look up.

stimuli.title: Kite Day
stimuli.text:
The first kite lasted eleven seconds. Sami counted. It climbed off the oval like something escaping, hung for a breath above the goalposts, then folded in half and dived into the long grass by the fence, where a magpie inspected it with obvious disgust.

"Too heavy in the tail," said a voice.

Mr Okafor, whose back fence ran along the edge of the oval, was leaning on it with his hat pulled low. He had been an engineer once, building bridges in places Sami had only seen in atlases, and now he spent his days building nothing at all, as far as Sami could tell, except tomato cages.

"I know," Sami said, although he hadn't known.

That night he rebuilt the kite at the kitchen table, alone, with the door shut. He used lighter dowel and less glue, and he trimmed the tail until it was hardly more than a ribbon. Kite Day was on Friday. Everyone in Year 6 would be on the oval, and Harrison Pike had already told the whole class that his kite was imported and could fly in a cyclone.

The second kite didn't fly at all. It spun on its string like a sycamore seed and slapped the ground, again and again, until one of the spars snapped.

Mr Okafor was at the fence again. This time he didn't say anything. He just held out his hand, palm up, and waited.

Sami looked at the broken kite. He looked at the hand, which was brown and creased and had a long white scar across the knuckles. Then he passed the kite over the fence.

They worked in Mr Okafor's shed for two afternoons. The old man asked questions instead of giving answers. What does the tail do? Why would a kite spin? Where is the wind pushing hardest? Sometimes Sami got the answers wrong, and Mr Okafor only nodded, as if a wrong answer were a useful thing to have found.

On Friday, Harrison Pike's imported kite tangled in a gum tree within five minutes. Sami's climbed and climbed until it was a red fleck against the blue, so high he had to tip his head right back to find it.

He looked over at the fence on the far side of the oval. A man in a hat raised one hand, then went back to his tomatoes.

stimuli.title: Ocean Pool, Winter
stimuli.text:
Nobody sensible swims in June.
The sand is cold as a dinner plate,
the wind comes off the water sharp
as a teacher's "Wait."

But here they are at half past six,
the regulars, in caps and goggles,
old men with chests like pale balloons,
two women laughing, bobbing like corks.

They do not race. They do not rush.
They swim the way the tide comes in:
slow, then slower, end to end,
as if the cold were no more than skin.

I stand in my hoodie, arms crossed tight,
and watch the steam rise off their backs.
One waves at me. "It's warmer in!"
she calls. The waves go out. Come back.

And I think how they must have been
nervous once, and young like me,
on some first morning, toes curled hard
against the edge, against the sea.

stimuli.title: Ghosts in the Gulf
stimuli.text:
Some of the most dangerous hunters in Australia's northern seas have no eyes, no brain and no hunger. They are fishing nets, lost or thrown away by boats, which drift for years on the ocean currents. Because they keep catching animals long after anyone is fishing with them, they are called ghost nets.

A single ghost net can be enormous. Some found washed up on beaches around the Gulf of Carpentaria have been hundreds of metres long and have weighed more than a small car. As they drift, they tangle turtles, sharks, dugongs and seabirds. Most of these animals drown, and their bodies attract more animals, which become trapped in turn.

The nets are a puzzle because most of them do not come from Australian boats. By studying the type of mesh and the ocean currents, researchers have shown that many nets drift here from fishing grounds in neighbouring seas. That means Australia cannot solve the problem alone.

On the coastline itself, much of the hard work is done by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander rangers, who patrol remote beaches, cut free trapped animals and haul nets above the high-tide line so that they cannot wash back out to sea. It is exhausting, unglamorous work, and it deserves far more recognition than it gets.

Some of the recovered net has found a surprising second life. Artists in Cape York and the Torres Strait weave it into sculptures of turtles, fish and other sea creatures, which have been shown in galleries around the world. Each sculpture is made from the very material that once killed the animals it shows.

Ghost nets will not disappear overnight. But better tracking of fishing gear, cooperation between countries and support for the people cleaning our beaches could turn the tide. It is a problem people created, and it is one people can fix.

stimuli.title: Wiring a Continent
stimuli.text:
In the 1860s, news from Britain took about two months to reach Australia, because it travelled by ship. Businesses, governments and families all had to wait. **[Gap 1]** The solution was a telegraph line, which could carry messages as pulses of electricity along a wire, almost instantly. Telegraph lines already linked several Australian cities, but none linked Australia with the rest of the world.

The plan was bold and expensive. An undersea cable already ran from Asia to the island of Java, and it could be extended to Darwin. **[Gap 2]** This meant building a line about 3,200 kilometres long across country that few European settlers had ever crossed. The route passed through the lands of many Aboriginal nations. The South Australian government took on the job and put it in the hands of Charles Todd, the colony's superintendent of telegraphs.

Work finally began in 1870. Teams cut poles from local timber, dug holes and strung wire, sometimes in temperatures above 40 degrees. **[Gap 3]** In the north, wet-season floods washed away supplies and left work parties stranded for weeks. Wire, insulators and food all had to be hauled huge distances by bullock teams and horses.

Another enemy was much smaller. **[Gap 4]** In those areas, many of the wooden poles were later replaced with iron ones, and some of those iron poles are still standing today.

The signal grew weaker as it travelled along the wire, so a message could not cross the whole distance in one go. **[Gap 5]** At each one, operators received the message and sent it on along the next section of the line. Some of these stations grew into towns, and Alice Springs began as one of them.

The line was completed in August 1872. **[Gap 6]** For the first time, a message from London could reach Adelaide in hours rather than months. Soon newspapers were printing news from Europe that was only a day or two old, and Australians felt a little less far away from the rest of the world.

stimuli.title: New Places
stimuli.text:
**Extract A**

Hi Jess,

We've been in Broken Hill for nine days now and it has been over 40 degrees for eight of them. Everything here is red: the dirt, the rocks, even the dog after he rolled in the yard. The nearest beach is hours and hours away by car. Mum says I'll get used to it, but I don't think I will. Did you make the netball team? Is Mr Fraser still giving spelling tests every Friday? Write back soon and tell me everything. I promise I'll come and stay in the summer holidays, even if I have to save up for the bus myself.

Love, Tilly

**Extract B**

Bogong moths make one of the most remarkable journeys of any Australian insect. Each spring, enormous numbers of them leave the plains of southern Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria and fly hundreds of kilometres to the Australian Alps. There they rest through the summer in cool, dark caves and rock crevices, away from the heat of the lowlands. In autumn they fly back to breed, and the following spring their young repeat the trip, even though they have never made it before. Scientists have found that the moths can use the stars and Earth's magnetic field to guide them. Bogong moths have also long been an important seasonal food for Aboriginal peoples of the region.

**Extract C**

I was seven when my family arrived in Australia, on a February afternoon so bright that I kept my eyes half shut all the way from the airport. The first thing I noticed when the taxi door opened was the smell: sharp and clean, like the cough lollies my grandmother kept in her handbag. Our new neighbour leaned over the fence and told my father we should come round "this arvo". I spent the rest of the day wondering what an arvo was, and whether we were supposed to bring one. I decided it was probably a kind of cake.

**Extract D**

The new house echoed. Every sound Maya made came back to her a little too loud: her footsteps, the tape tearing off the boxes, the sigh she hadn't meant to let out. Her room was empty except for a mattress and a lamp. Then, behind the door, she noticed the pencil lines. Someone had measured children against the doorframe, year after year: KATIE 5, BEN 4, KATIE 6, BEN 7, KATIE 9. Maya stood with her back against the wood, laid a ruler flat on her head and reached for a pencil. MAYA 11, she wrote, a little apart from the others, but on the same frame.

stimuli.title: Homework
stimuli.text:
**Text 1**

*Give Us Our Afternoons Back*

Every afternoon this term I have had a worksheet. Fractions on Monday, spelling on Tuesday, a "research task" on Wednesday that was really just copying from a website. By the time I finish, it is getting dark, and I have missed footy training, missed the park and missed talking to my family at dinner. I am not lazy. I work hard all day at school. When I get home, I want to kick a ball, build something, or read a book because I want to, not because there is a box to tick. Reading is the one kind of homework I would happily keep, because I would do it anyway. The rest should go. Isn't childhood supposed to have some time in it that belongs to us?

**Text 2**

*What Does Homework Actually Do?*

Few school topics cause as many arguments at the dinner table as homework. Researchers who have reviewed many studies have found that, for high school students, homework is linked to better results. For primary school students, the link is much weaker, and long worksheets show little benefit. That does not mean homework should vanish. Regular reading at home is strongly linked to wider vocabulary and better comprehension, and short practice of basic skills such as times tables can help them stick. A sensible approach for primary schools may be a little reading each night, some practice when it is genuinely useful, and plenty of time left over for play, sport and family. The goal of homework, after all, should be learning, not simply keeping children busy.

stimuli.title: The Roof Nobody Could Build
stimuli.text:
When the Danish architect Jørn Utzon won the competition to design a new opera house for Sydney in 1957, his entry was little more than a set of beautiful sketches. The judges loved the soaring white roofs, which looked like sails filling with wind above the harbour. There was just one problem: nobody knew how to build them.

The shells in Utzon's drawings were free-flowing curves, each one a different shape. In the days before powerful computers, engineers had no way to calculate how such curves would carry their own enormous weight. For years, Utzon and the engineers tried design after design. Some were too heavy, and some could not be built at a sensible cost. The project fell behind, and the bills grew.

The breakthrough came in about 1961. Utzon realised that if every shell was cut from the surface of one imaginary sphere, the curves would all match. The roof could then be built from repeated concrete pieces, made on the ground and lifted into place, like parts of a giant kit. A popular story says the idea came to him while he was peeling an orange, but there is no proof that it really happened that way.

The roofs were finally covered with more than a million tiles, glazed so that they shine in sunlight without too much glare. Utzon left the project in 1966 after disagreements with the government, and he never returned to see it finished. The Opera House opened in 1973 and is now one of the most recognised buildings in the world.

stimuli.title: Learning Something New
stimuli.text:
**Extract A**

Day 3 of skateboarding. Today I made it all the way down the driveway without falling off, which would be more impressive if I hadn't then rolled straight into the letterbox. Scraped knee, ripped shorts, very sore pride. Dad says every skater has a letterbox story. Tomorrow I'm going to try turning, preferably away from the letterbox.

**Extract B**

To learn to juggle, start with a single ball. Toss it from hand to hand in a gentle arc that peaks at about eye level. When you can do this twenty times without a drop, add a second ball: throw the first, and as it peaks, throw the second underneath it. Only move on to three balls once two feel easy. Expect to drop them often. Everyone does.

**Extract C**

My grandmother learned to swim at sixty-eight. She had grown up far from any beach or pool, and she had spent forty years sitting on the sand while the rest of us swam. Then one summer she simply began. She watched the toddlers in the shallow end, copied their kicks, and ignored anyone who stared. By autumn she could swim a full length, slowly, with her chin held high.

**Extract D**

When Ms Patel asked if anyone in the class could speak French, Leo's hand went up before his brain could stop it. "Oui," he said confidently. It was, unfortunately, most of the French he knew. For the rest of the lesson he nodded wisely whenever she spoke, and when she asked him to introduce himself, he had a very long coughing fit.

questions.stem: Nell "didn't ask for help. That was the annoying part." Why does this annoy Jai?
options: She works more slowly than he would
She no longer seems to need him
She ignores the advice in her book
questions.explanation: The next sentences explain it: Nell "had always asked Jai for help", so her new independence leaves him feeling unneeded. Nothing suggests she is slow or noisy; he watches her work "in long, patient strokes".

questions.stem: When Nell says the dinghy "needs someone to bail", she means it needs someone to
questions.explanation: Jai's reply, "So it still leaks?", shows that bailing means getting rid of water that comes in. Steering and sailing are jobs on a boat, but they do not connect to a leak.

questions.stem: Nell runs her palm across the patch "the way you might stroke a sleeping dog". This comparison suggests that she
options: is checking the patch for more possums
is too tired to press hard
questions.explanation: Stroking a sleeping dog is a slow, gentle, loving action, so the simile shows her affection and care for the boat she has repaired. It is a comparison, not a sign that she really believes the boat is alive.

questions.stem: What does the sentence "Neither of them mentioned that he had said she'd never finish" suggest?
options: They both chose to let it pass
Nell was still hurt by his words
Nell never heard him say it
questions.explanation: "Neither of them mentioned" shows both remember it but quietly agree not to bring it up, which fits the peace offering of the cordial. Nell heard him, since he said it to her face, and she is calm and friendly, not hurt.

questions.stem: Which word best describes the tone of the final conversation between Nell and Jai?
questions.explanation: Nell "grinned" and teases Jai that bailing is "what you're for", so the tone is light and joking. Nothing in the exchange is angry, worried or stiff.

questions.stem: What is the extract mainly about?
options: a girl learning to sail on a lake
a boy who is jealous of his sister's friends
a shared project bringing siblings closer
a family fixing a boat for a holiday
questions.explanation: The story moves from Jai doubting Nell to helping her and being invited on the boat: the repair draws them together. Nell has not sailed yet (the lake trip is "next weekend"), so the extract is not about learning to sail.

questions.stem: The paddocks are compared to "an old dog's coat, worn thin and grey". This suggests the paddocks are
questions.explanation: A coat "worn thin and grey" has lost its colour and has bald spots, like dry paddocks after "eleven months" without rain. The poem is about drought, so flooded or thick grass cannot fit.

questions.stem: What does the line "the dam was a mirror cracked in two" suggest about the dam?
options: It had dried out and split
It was full and perfectly still
It had been broken by a storm
questions.explanation: A mirror is a smooth surface, and "cracked" shows the dried mud has split apart, which matches the drought in the first stanza. A still, full dam would not be cracked, and the storm does not come until later in the poem.

questions.stem: Dad "tapped the glass and checked again, / as if a stare could make it fill." What do these lines show about Dad?
options: He thinks the gauge is broken
He is angry at the weather
questions.explanation: "As if a stare could make it fill" shows he is hoping so hard that he keeps checking, even though looking cannot bring rain. Tapping the glass might seem like checking for a fault, but the second line makes clear it is longing, not a broken gauge.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the repetition in "And then it fell. It fell and fell"?
options: It shows the speaker is bored
It shows the rain kept coming
It makes the storm seem brief
It suggests the rain is gentle
questions.explanation: Repeating "fell" mimics rain that goes on and on, and the next lines list everything it soaks. The rain "drummed the shed" and "filled each rut", so it is neither brief nor gentle.

questions.stem: In the final stanza Dad stands in the rain "face up, the way some people pray". This suggests he feels
questions.explanation: Comparing him to someone praying shows quiet gratitude and relief that the drought has broken. He is "not running in, not minding" the soaking, so he is not afraid or embarrassed.

questions.stem: What is the writer's main purpose?
options: to argue that trees are essential
to explain how leaves make food
to warn that roots damage footpaths
to describe a summer walk in Sydney
questions.explanation: The article ends by saying we must treat trees "as infrastructure, as necessary as water pipes", so it is persuading readers. Roots lifting footpaths is mentioned only as a small problem that can be managed.

questions.stem: Which of these ideas from the article is an opinion rather than a fact?
options: Roads and roofs soak up the sun's heat
Trees release water through their leaves
Some councils have set canopy targets
A shadeless suburb is designed for cars
questions.explanation: Saying a suburb without shade is "designed for cars, not people" is the writer's judgement and cannot be proved. The other three can be checked by measuring or looking up council plans.

questions.stem: Which detail does the writer use to show that streets without trees are hotter?
options: the cost of running air conditioning
questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives measured footpath temperatures "more than 20 degrees higher" in full sun. Planting targets are a response to the problem, not evidence that bare streets are hotter.

questions.stem: According to the article, why do some suburbs "never really cool down"?
options: Air conditioners run through the night
Roads and roofs give off heat at night
Houses fill every square metre of land
questions.explanation: The article says roads, roofs and car parks "soak up the sun's heat during the day and release it slowly at night". Small blocks are mentioned later, as the reason trees are lost, not as the reason for night heat.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the paragraph beginning "Of course, trees are not perfect neighbours"?
options: to admit problems but play them down
to change the writer's whole argument
to list the best trees to plant
to explain how trees cool the air
questions.explanation: The paragraph names real drawbacks (roots and leaves) and then calls them "small ones" that "can be managed", which answers objections without giving up the argument. It does not name any species, so it is not a list of trees.

questions.stem: Planting a tree is easy, but keeping it alive is harder. [[1]], a sapling planted in a dry spell may need about 20 litres of water a week. [[2]] it is watered deeply, its roots stay near the surface and it struggles in the next heatwave. A little effort in the first two summers can [[3]] a tree that will shade the street for a century.
questions.explanation: "For example" introduces a case of how hard care can be; there is no contrast for "However". "Unless" fits because shallow roots happen only when deep watering is missing. Effort in the early years can "save" a tree; "harm" or "replace" would contradict the point of the paragraph.

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 1?
options: Electric signals travel faster than ripples, so the two arrive at different times.
A platypus may eat up to a fifth of its own body weight in a single night.
Because it is shy and active mostly at night, it is hard to know how many are left.
When it dives, it shuts its eyes, ears and nostrils tight.
Female platypuses lay one to three small, leathery eggs in a burrow.
questions.explanation: The next sentence says scientists could not understand "how it caught anything at all", which only makes sense once we know it hunts with its eyes, ears and nostrils shut. The egg-laying sentence is true of platypuses but has nothing to do with hunting.

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 2?
options: When it dives, it shuts its eyes, ears and nostrils tight.
Many of these sensors can detect very weak electric fields.
Electric signals travel faster than ripples, so the two arrive at different times.
When its pouches are full, it rises to breathe.
Female platypuses lay one to three small, leathery eggs in a burrow.
questions.explanation: "These sensors" points back to the "tiny sensors" in the bill, and the next sentence explains the "faint electric signal" that prey give off. The sentence about the two signals arriving "at different times" cannot go here, because ripples have not been mentioned yet.

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 3?
options: When it dives, it shuts its eyes, ears and nostrils tight.
A platypus may eat up to a fifth of its own body weight in a single night.
Because it is shy and active mostly at night, it is hard to know how many are left.
Female platypuses lay one to three small, leathery eggs in a burrow.
Electric signals travel faster than ripples, so the two arrive at different times.
questions.explanation: The gap comes after ripples are introduced and before "compare the two" and the lightning and thunder comparison; only this sentence explains why two signals arriving at different times are useful. None of the other options mentions two signals.

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 4?
options: A platypus may eat up to a fifth of its own body weight in a single night.
When it dives, it shuts its eyes, ears and nostrils tight.
When its pouches are full, it rises to breathe.
Because it is shy and active mostly at night, it is hard to know how many are left.
Female platypuses lay one to three small, leathery eggs in a burrow.
questions.explanation: "That would be like a 40-kilogram child eating eight kilograms of food" needs an amount to compare: a fifth of its body weight. The sentence also follows on from "a great deal of energy".

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 5?
options: When it dives, it shuts its eyes, ears and nostrils tight.
Many of these sensors can detect very weak electric fields.
When its pouches are full, it rises to breathe.
A platypus may eat up to a fifth of its own body weight in a single night.
Because it is shy and active mostly at night, it is hard to know how many are left.
questions.explanation: The platypus has just filled its cheek pouches underwater, and the next sentence begins "Then it floats on the surface", so the gap must bring it up from the riverbed. The diving sentence describes going down, the opposite movement.

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 6?
options: Many of these sensors can detect very weak electric fields.
Electric signals travel faster than ripples, so the two arrive at different times.
A platypus may eat up to a fifth of its own body weight in a single night.
Because it is shy and active mostly at night, it is hard to know how many are left.
Female platypuses lay one to three small, leathery eggs in a burrow.
questions.explanation: The next sentence says volunteers survey platypuses "to find out whether their numbers are falling", which answers the problem that it is "hard to know how many are left". The egg-laying sentence fits the topic but not this paragraph about threats and numbers.

questions.stem: Which extract describes a plan that went wrong?
questions.explanation: In Extract A, Dad's "famous shortcut added two hours" and the track "simply stopped". Ari in Extract D gets lost because of fog, not because of a plan.

questions.stem: Which extract gives the reader advice to follow?
questions.explanation: Extract B speaks directly to "you" with instructions such as "stop", "find shelter" and "tell someone where you are going". The others tell stories rather than advise.

questions.stem: In which extract does the writer change their mind about a past event?
questions.explanation: The writer of Extract C once told the story "as proof of how brave I was" but now thinks "it is really a story about her". Extract A records the day it happened, so there is no later rethinking.

questions.stem: In which extract does someone work out a direction by listening?
questions.explanation: Ari hears the waves "on her left" and reasons that the road "had to be on her right". The whistle in Extract B is for calling rescuers, not for finding the way.

questions.stem: In which extract are supplies used up too early?
questions.explanation: Sam "had eaten all the scroggin by eleven o'clock", leaving one apple for lunch. Extract B mentions drinking water "if you have it" but describes no one running out.

questions.stem: In which extract is someone more upset than the person who was lost?
questions.explanation: The child "did not cry", but the grandmother "was the one in tears". In Extract D the uncle is calm, simply saying "Took your time".

questions.stem: Which extract explains how a lost person might be seen from the air?
questions.explanation: Extract B says bright clothing or something shiny "will make you easier to spot from a helicopter". None of the other extracts mentions searching from above.

questions.stem: In which extract does weather cause someone to lose their way?
questions.explanation: The fog in Extract D makes the car park, path and fence vanish. In Extract A the family get sunburnt, but they are lost because of the shortcut, not the weather.

questions.stem: Which extract was written while the writer was travelling?
questions.explanation: The diary writer says "I'm writing this in the back seat on the drive home". Extract C looks back from many years later.

questions.stem: Which extract is told by an adult looking back on their childhood?
questions.explanation: Extract C begins "I was six" and refers to "children of my own", so an adult is remembering. Extract A is a child's diary written on the same day.

questions.stem: Which idea is found in both texts?
options: Sea turtles are harmed by streetlights
City lights hide much of the night sky
Stars once guided when to plant crops
Country roads should stay unlit at night
questions.explanation: Text 1's speaker can see only "four stars" from a city window, and Text 2 says more than a third of people "can no longer see the Milky Way from home". Turtles appear only in Text 2 and planting by the stars only in Text 1.

questions.stem: How does the attitude of the speaker in Text 1 differ from that of the writer of Text 2?
options: Text 1 is bored; Text 2 is excited
Text 1 is angry; Text 2 is amused
Text 1 is fearful; Text 2 is hopeless
Text 1 is awed; Text 2 is practical
questions.explanation: The speaker in Text 1 is amazed ("And there it is") and stands with "neck aching", while Text 2 explains a problem and practical fixes. Text 2 calls it "one of the easiest kinds of pollution to fix", so it is not hopeless.

questions.stem: Which text compares the night sky to something found in a kitchen?
questions.explanation: Text 1 describes the Milky Way "like flour across a dark bench". Text 2 uses facts and does not compare the sky to anything in a kitchen.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the purpose of each text?
options: Text 1 shares a moment; Text 2 explains a problem
Text 1 explains a problem; Text 2 shares a moment
Text 1 gives directions; Text 2 tells a story
questions.explanation: Text 1 captures one night with Gran, while Text 2 sets out the harm done by light pollution and how to fix it. The first wrong option simply swaps the two purposes.

questions.stem: How would the writer of Text 2 most likely view the sky that Gran shows the speaker in Text 1?
options: as an example of light pollution
as a danger to migrating birds
as what many people have lost
as a reason to light the road
questions.explanation: Text 2 is titled "Losing the Dark" and says most people cannot see the Milky Way; Gran's dark sky, "out past the last streetlight", is exactly what city dwellers are missing. It is the opposite of light pollution.
Line up the decimal points: 3.40 + 0.75 = 4.15, and 4.15 + 12 = 16.15. 4.27 comes from treating 12 as 0.12.

questions.stem: A rectangle is 12 cm long and 7.5 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: Perimeter = 2 × (12 + 7.5) = 39 cm. 19.5 cm adds only one length and one width, and 90 is the area.

questions.stem: What is $48 \div 6 \times 2 + 3^2$?
questions.explanation: Square first, then divide and multiply from left to right: 48 ÷ 6 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16, and 16 + 9 = 25. 13 comes from doing 6 × 2 before the division.

questions.stem: Five quiz scores are 7, 9, 4, 10 and 5. What is the mean score?
questions.explanation: The scores add to 35, and 35 ÷ 5 = 7. 35 is the total, not the mean.

questions.stem: A jacket costs \$80. In a sale its price is reduced by 15%. What is the sale price?
questions.explanation: 15% of \$80 is \$12, so the sale price is \$80 − \$12 = \$68. \$12 is the discount, not the price.

questions.stem: Mia and Leo share 45 marbles in the ratio 4 : 5. How many marbles does Leo get?
questions.explanation: There are 4 + 5 = 9 parts, so one part is 45 ÷ 9 = 5 marbles. Leo gets 5 parts, 25 marbles; 20 is Mia's share.

questions.stem: How many millilitres are there in 2.35 litres?
At 6 am the temperature at a ski resort was −4 °C. By noon it had risen 11 degrees, and by 10 pm it had fallen 9 degrees from the noon temperature. What was the temperature at 10 pm?
questions.explanation: −4 + 11 = 7 at noon, then 7 − 9 = −2 °C. 2 °C comes from ignoring that the start was below zero.

questions.stem: A train leaves the city at 10:47 am and arrives in the mountains at 12:29 pm. How long is the trip?
questions.explanation: From 10:47 to 11:47 is 1 hour, and from 11:47 to 12:29 is 42 minutes. 1 h 18 min comes from subtracting the minutes the wrong way round (47 − 29).

questions.stem: A bag holds 4 red, 5 blue and 3 green marbles. One marble is taken without looking. What is the probability that it is not blue?
questions.explanation: There are 12 marbles and 4 + 3 = 7 are not blue, so the probability is 7/12. 5/12 is the chance that it is blue.

questions.stem: What is $0.4 \times 0.06$?
questions.explanation: 4 × 6 = 24, and the two factors have 1 + 2 = 3 decimal places, so the answer is 0.024.

questions.stem: Which is closest to $398 \times 51$?
questions.explanation: Round to 400 × 50 = 20 000. The exact answer is 20 298.

questions.stem: A garden is a rectangle 10 m long and 8 m wide with a 4 m by 3 m rectangle of paving cut out of one corner. What area of the garden is left for plants?
questions.explanation: The whole rectangle is 10 × 8 = 80 m², and the paving takes 4 × 3 = 12 m², leaving 68 m². 92 adds the paving instead of taking it away.

questions.stem: Which of these fractions is the largest?
The mean of four numbers is 15. Three of the numbers are 12, 18 and 9. What is the fourth number?
questions.explanation: Four numbers with a mean of 15 add to 60. 12 + 18 + 9 = 39, so the fourth is 60 − 39 = 21.

questions.stem: What is the next number in this pattern? 1, 4, 13, 40, ...
questions.explanation: Each number is three times the one before, plus 1: 40 × 3 + 1 = 121. 67 adds the last gap of 27 again, but the gaps triple (3, 9, 27, 81).

questions.stem: One bus leaves the depot every 12 minutes and another every 18 minutes. Both leave together at 8:00 am. When do they next leave together?
questions.explanation: The lowest common multiple of 12 and 18 is 36, so they leave together again 36 minutes later. 11:36 am comes from multiplying 12 × 18 = 216 minutes.

questions.stem: Six seedlings are measured in centimetres: 14, 9, 21, 17, 12 and 20. What is the median height?
questions.explanation: In order: 9, 12, 14, 17, 20, 21. With six values the median is halfway between the middle two, (14 + 17) ÷ 2 = 15.5 cm. 12 is the range.

questions.stem: Which number is a factor of 84 but not a factor of 63?
questions.explanation: 84 = 4 × 21, but 63 ÷ 4 is not a whole number. 7, 21 and 3 divide both numbers, and 9 divides 63 but not 84.

questions.stem: A flight leaves Sydney at 21:50 and takes 5 hours 25 minutes. Using Sydney time, when does it land?
questions.explanation: 21:50 + 5 h = 02:50 the next day, and 25 more minutes makes 03:15.

questions.stem: In a class of 56 students, 3/8 walk to school. Of the students who do not walk, 1/5 ride a bike. How many students ride a bike?
questions.explanation: 3/8 of 56 is 21, so 35 students do not walk. 1/5 of 35 is 7. 21 is the number who walk.

questions.stem: How many prime numbers are there between 30 and 50?
questions.explanation: The primes are 31, 37, 41, 43 and 47. 39 (3 × 13) and 49 (7 × 7) look prime but are not.

questions.stem: One angle of a triangle is 47°. A second angle is twice as large as the first. What is the size of the third angle?
questions.explanation: The second angle is 94°, and the three angles add to 180°: 180 − 47 − 94 = 39°. 86° forgets the second angle is doubled.

questions.stem: Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. One angle is 4 times the size of the other. What is the size of the smaller angle?
questions.explanation: Angles on a straight line add to 180°. The two angles are 5 equal parts, so one part is 180 ÷ 5 = 36°. 45° uses 4 parts instead of 5.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides 18 km in 45 minutes. What is her average speed in kilometres per hour?
questions.explanation: 45 minutes is 3/4 of an hour, so in a full hour she would ride 18 ÷ 3 × 4 = 24 km. 13.5 multiplies by 3/4 instead of dividing.

questions.stem: The same number goes in both boxes: $7 \times \square - 15 = 4 \times \square + 12$. What is the number?
questions.explanation: Taking 4 lots of the number from both sides leaves 3 lots − 15 = 12, so 3 lots = 27 and the number is 9. Check: 63 − 15 = 48 and 36 + 12 = 48.

questions.stem: A school had 250 students last year and has 290 this year. By what percentage did the number of students increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is 40, and 40 out of the original 250 is 40/250 = 16%. 40% confuses the number of students with the percentage.

questions.stem: A map has a scale of 1 : 25 000. Two lookouts are 6 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they in real life?
questions.explanation: 6 × 25 000 = 150 000 cm. That is 1500 m, or 1.5 km. 150 m drops a zero when converting centimetres to metres.

questions.stem: Three consecutive even numbers add to 78. What is the largest of the three?
questions.explanation: The middle number is 78 ÷ 3 = 26, so the numbers are 24, 26 and 28. 26 is the middle one, not the largest.

questions.stem: A fish tank is 60 cm long, 30 cm wide and 40 cm high. It is filled with water to 5 cm below the top. How many litres of water are in it? (1000 cm³ = 1 L)
questions.explanation: The water is 35 cm deep: 60 × 30 × 35 = 63 000 cm³, which is 63 L. 72 L is the full tank.

questions.stem: A shop sells rice in five sizes. Which size is the best value?
questions.explanation: Compare the price of 100 g: 750 g costs 64c per 100 g, against 70c, 69c, 66c and 68c for the others. The 2 kg bag at 66c is close but dearer.

questions.stem:
A school play charges \$12 for an adult ticket and \$7 for a child ticket.

| Night | Adult tickets | Child tickets |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | 15 | 20 |
| Tuesday | 22 | 10 |
| Wednesday | 18 | 26 |

How much more money was taken on Wednesday than on Monday?
questions.explanation: Monday took 15 × \$12 + 20 × \$7 = \$320. Wednesday took 18 × \$12 + 26 × \$7 = \$398. The difference is \$78; \$64 is Wednesday compared with Tuesday.

questions.stem: In a survey of 30 students, 12 chose cricket, 9 chose soccer and the rest chose netball. The results are shown in a pie chart. What is the angle of the netball sector?
questions.explanation: 30 − 12 − 9 = 9 students chose netball, which is 9/30 of the circle: 9/30 × 360° = 108°. 144° is the cricket sector.

questions.stem: A solid cube 4 cm on each edge is painted on all six faces, then cut into 1 cm cubes. How many of the small cubes have paint on exactly two faces?
questions.explanation: Small cubes with two painted faces lie along the edges but not at the corners. Each of the 12 edges has 4 − 2 = 2 of them, so 24. The 8 corner cubes have three painted faces.

questions.stem: Lily has 20 coins, all 20c and 50c coins. Together they are worth \$6.40. How many 50c coins does she have?
questions.explanation: If all 20 coins were 20c they would make \$4.00. Each swap to a 50c coin adds 30c, and \$2.40 ÷ 30c = 8 swaps. Check: 8 × 50c + 12 × 20c = \$4.00 + \$2.40.

questions.stem:
Mr Okafor: Our school should put a water fountain beside the oval. Students who play sport at lunch come back to class thirsty, and thirsty students find it hard to concentrate.

Which one of these statements, if true, most strengthens Mr Okafor's argument?
options: The nearest water fountain is a five minute walk from the oval.
Most students carry a full water bottle with them to the oval.
The oval was planted with new grass at the start of the year.
Some students would rather spend lunch in the library than outside.
questions.explanation: If the closest fountain is far away, thirsty students really do lack an easy drink, so a fountain by the oval would help. Students already carrying full bottles would weaken the argument, and the grass and the library are beside the point.

questions.stem:
Five friends compare their heights. Aisha is taller than Ben. Ben is taller than Callum. Dev is shorter than Callum. Ella is taller than Aisha.

Who is the third tallest?
questions.explanation: From tallest to shortest the order is Ella, Aisha, Ben, Callum, Dev. So Ben is third.

questions.stem:
Tom: Our class goldfish has stopped eating much. It must be sick, so we should take it to the vet.

Which one of these statements, if true, most weakens Tom's argument?
options: The goldfish has also started to swim slowly near the bottom.
Goldfish eat less when their water is cold, and it is now winter.
The vet nearest to the school is closed on Saturdays and Sundays.
The class bought the goldfish from a pet shop two years ago.
questions.explanation: This gives a healthy reason for the fish eating less, so it may not be sick at all. Swimming slowly near the bottom would make sickness more likely, which strengthens Tom's argument instead.

questions.stem: A movie starts at 6:45 pm and runs for 1 hour and 50 minutes. What time does it finish?
questions.explanation: 6:45 pm plus 1 hour is 7:45 pm, and 50 more minutes is 8:35 pm. Forgetting to carry into the next hour gives 7:35 pm.

questions.stem:
Ellie: Everyone who won a prize at the art show used paint. I used paint, so I must win a prize.

Which one of the following shows the mistake Ellie has made?
options: Ellie did not check how many people entered the art show.
Some prize winners might have used pencils as well as paint.
Many people who used paint may still not win a prize.
Ellie thinks the judges like paintings more than drawings.
questions.explanation: The winners all used paint, but that does not mean everyone who used paint wins. Ellie has turned the rule around. The number of entries does not fix that mistake.

questions.stem: Leila has 20 dollars. She buys 3 notebooks that cost 4 dollars each and a pen that costs 3 dollars. How much money does she have left?
questions.explanation: The notebooks cost 3 times 4, which is 12 dollars, and with the pen she spends 15 dollars. 20 minus 15 leaves 5 dollars. Forgetting the pen gives 8 dollars.

questions.stem:
Lachlan: It is going to rain on Saturday, so our cricket match will be cancelled.

Which assumption has Lachlan made?
options: Lachlan's team was likely to win the cricket match.
The weather forecast is usually wrong about Saturdays.
The cricket match was due to start in the morning.
Cricket matches are cancelled when it rains.
questions.explanation: Lachlan only gets from rain to a cancelled match if rain causes matches to be called off. A wrong forecast would work against his argument, not support it.

questions.stem:
What number comes next in this sequence?

3, 7, 15, 31, ?
questions.explanation: Each number is double the one before plus 1: 31 times 2 is 62, plus 1 is 63. Adding 16 as if the jumps were equal gives 47.

questions.stem:
Every student in the chess club also plays in the school band. Ruby is in the chess club.

If the information is true, which one of these statements must also be true?
options: Ruby plays in the school band.
Ruby is the best chess player.
Everyone in the band plays chess.
Ruby does not play any sport.
questions.explanation: Ruby is in the chess club and every chess club member plays in the band, so Ruby does. The rule does not work backwards, so band members need not be in the chess club.

questions.stem: Today is Tuesday. What day of the week will it be 17 days from today?
questions.explanation: 14 days from Tuesday is Tuesday again. 3 more days is Friday.

questions.stem:
The canteen sells sushi only on Wednesdays. Today the canteen is selling sushi.

Kiara says: "So today must be Wednesday."
Ben says: "So the canteen will not sell sushi tomorrow."

If the information is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.explanation: Sushi is sold only on Wednesdays, so today is Wednesday, as Kiara says. Tomorrow is Thursday, so there will be no sushi, as Ben says. Both are correct.

questions.stem: Kai has 3 T-shirts and 4 pairs of shorts. How many different outfits of one T-shirt and one pair of shorts can he make?
questions.explanation: Each of the 3 T-shirts can go with any of the 4 pairs of shorts, so there are 3 times 4, which is 12 outfits. Adding instead of multiplying gives 7.

questions.stem:
Priya: Our class should hold the cake stall on Friday instead of Monday. More parents come to school on Fridays because that is when the weekly assembly is held, and parents buy most of the cakes.

Which one of these statements, if true, most strengthens Priya's argument?
options: Many parents leave straight after assembly to get to work on time.
Parents at assembly usually stay at school for a while afterwards.
The class baked more chocolate cakes than lemon cakes last time.
Students in other classes also like to buy cakes from the stall.
questions.explanation: Priya needs the Friday parents to still be around when the stall is open, and this shows they are. Parents rushing off after assembly would weaken her point, and the type of cake or other buyers says nothing about Friday versus Monday.

questions.stem:
The table shows how many laps four students swam this week.

| Name | Mon | Tue | Wed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zoe | 6 | 4 | 5 |
| Omar | 3 | 7 | 6 |
| Bella | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| Tariq | 8 | 2 | 4 |

The coach gives a badge to anyone who swam at least 15 laps in total and at least 4 laps every day. Who gets a badge?
questions.explanation: The totals are Zoe 15, Omar 16, Bella 15 and Tariq 14. Omar has the highest total but swam only 3 laps on Monday, so only Zoe and Bella meet both rules.

questions.stem:
Jasmine: The library should buy more graphic novels. They are always borrowed, so students clearly love reading them.

Which one of these statements, if true, most weakens Jasmine's argument?
options: Many students ask the librarian when new graphic novels will arrive.
Graphic novels cost about the same as other books in the library.
One student borrows every graphic novel each week for a project.
The library also lends magazines and audio books to students.
questions.explanation: If one student is doing all the borrowing, the books being always out does not show that students in general love them. Students asking for new ones would support Jasmine instead.

questions.stem: Noor thinks of a number. She doubles it, then subtracts 6, then halves the result. Her answer is 11. What number did she start with?
questions.explanation: Work backwards: 11 doubled is 22, add 6 to get 28, and halve to get 14. Check: 14 doubled is 28, minus 6 is 22, halved is 11.

questions.stem:
Marcus: I asked five friends in my class whether the school should have a longer lunch break, and all five said yes. So nearly every student at our school wants a longer lunch.

Which one of the following shows the mistake Marcus has made?
options: Marcus should have asked the teachers instead of the students.
A longer lunch might make the school day finish later.
Marcus did not say how much longer the lunch break should be.
Five friends in one class cannot speak for a whole school.
questions.explanation: Five friends from one class may think alike and cannot show what hundreds of students want. A later finish might be a reason against the idea, but it is not a mistake in his reasoning.

questions.stem: Josh is 4 years older than his sister Mila. In 3 years' time, their ages will add up to 30. How old is Mila now?
questions.explanation: In 3 years their ages add to 30 and differ by 4, so they will be 13 and 17. Mila will be 13 then, so she is 10 now. Answering 13 forgets to go back 3 years.

questions.stem:
Ms Nguyen: Zara has finished all her maths homework early this week, so she will have time to help paint the class mural.

Which assumption has Ms Nguyen made?
options: Zara has nothing else she needs to do in her spare time.
Painting a mural takes less time than doing maths homework.
Zara is the best painter in the whole class.
The mural needs to be finished by the end of the week.
questions.explanation: Finishing homework only frees up time if Zara has no other jobs or activities filling it. Ms Nguyen does not need Zara to be the best painter, only to have time.

questions.stem:
Five students sit in a row of chairs numbered 1 to 5 from left to right. Grace sits in chair 3. Liam sits directly to the left of Grace. Sofia is not at either end. Hamid sits somewhere to the right of Sofia.

Where does Jae sit?
questions.explanation: Liam is in chair 2. Sofia cannot be at an end, so she takes chair 4, and Hamid must be to her right in chair 5. That leaves chair 1 for Jae.

questions.stem:
At Bayside Public School, every student who walks to school gets a green token. Some students who get a green token also get a gold token. Ahmed did not get a green token.

If the information is true, which one of these statements must also be true?
options: Ahmed came to school by car.
Ahmed did not walk to school.
Ahmed did not get a gold token.
questions.explanation: If Ahmed had walked he would have a green token, so he did not walk. He might have come by bus rather than car, and nothing says gold tokens only go to green token holders, so either gold option could be wrong.

questions.stem:
One of three children ate the last biscuit. Exactly one of them is telling the truth.

Ruby: "Sam ate it."
Sam: "I did not eat it."
Tia: "Ruby did not eat it."

Who ate the biscuit?
questions.explanation: If Ruby ate it, only Sam's statement is true, which fits. If Sam ate it, Ruby and Tia are both telling the truth, and if Tia ate it, Sam and Tia are both telling the truth. So it was Ruby.

questions.stem:
In Mia's class, everyone who plays the violin also learns French. Nobody who learns French is in the drama group.

If the information is true, which one of these statements cannot be true?
options: Mia plays the violin and learns French.
Leo learns French but does not play the violin.
Ivy plays the violin and is in the drama group.
Sam is in the drama group and does not learn French.
questions.explanation: A violin player learns French, and nobody who learns French is in drama, so a violin player cannot be in drama. Each of the other statements fits the rules.

questions.stem: In a secret code, each letter is replaced by the letter two places after it in the alphabet, so A becomes C and Y becomes A. A code word is written as FQI. What is the real word?
questions.explanation: To decode, move each letter two places back: F becomes D, Q becomes O and I becomes G, giving DOG. Moving forward instead gives HSK.

questions.stem:
To join the coding club, a student must be in Year 5 or Year 6 and must have handed in a permission note. Isla is in Year 6 and is in the coding club. Raj is in Year 6 and has handed in a permission note.

Noah says: "Isla must have handed in a permission note."
Chloe says: "Raj must be in the coding club."

If the information is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.explanation: Every club member must have handed in a note, so Noah is right about Isla. Raj meets the rules for joining, but nothing says he chose to join, so Chloe is wrong.

questions.stem: A bus leaves the depot every 25 minutes, starting at 6:10 am. Kim arrives at the depot at 8:00 am. How long must she wait for the next bus?
questions.explanation: The buses leave at 6:10, 6:35, 7:00, 7:25, 7:50 and 8:15. Kim just misses the 7:50 bus, so she waits 15 minutes.

questions.stem:
Mrs Silva's class has a rule: if it rains at lunch, students play in the hall. Today students played in the hall.

Jack says: "So it must have rained at lunch today."
Mei says: "Students might have played in the hall even if it had not rained."

If the information is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.explanation: The rule only says what happens when it rains. It does not say the hall is used only on rainy days, so Jack cannot be sure, while Mei is right that it might not have rained.

questions.stem: Six teams enter a netball competition. Each team plays every other team once. How many games are played?
questions.explanation: The first team plays 5 games, the next has 4 new opponents, then 3, 2 and 1: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15. Counting 6 times 5 gives 30, but that counts every game twice.

questions.stem: How many whole numbers from 1 to 100 contain the digit 7 at least once?
questions.explanation: Ten numbers end in 7 (7, 17 ... 97) and ten are in the seventies (70 to 79). 77 is in both lists, so the total is 10 + 10 - 1 = 19.

questions.stem:
Coach Lena: Our netball team lost most of its games in the second half this season. The players must be getting too tired by then, so we should add more running to training.

Which one of these statements, if true, most strengthens Coach Lena's argument?
options: Opposing teams usually changed their tactics at half time.
The team trains on the school courts twice a week after school.
The team won more games this season than it did last season.
Fresh players brought on late in games played as well as ever.
questions.explanation: If rested players did fine in the second half, tiredness looks like the real cause, which supports more fitness work. Other teams changing tactics gives a different cause and so weakens the argument.

questions.stem:
Principal Harris: Since we started giving out stickers for walking to school, the number of students who walk has gone up. The stickers are clearly working.

Which one of these statements, if true, most weakens Principal Harris's argument?
options: A new footpath to the school opened the same week the stickers began.
Students who walk say they are saving their stickers to swap for prizes.
Students who walk arrive at about the same time as those driven.
Some students live too far away from the school to walk there.
questions.explanation: The new footpath could explain the extra walkers, so the stickers may not be the reason. Students saving stickers for prizes suggests the stickers do matter, which supports the principal.

questions.stem:
Six runners finished a race with no ties. Uma finished after Pia but before Rhys. Kofi finished directly after Rhys. Nadia finished before Pia. Lou finished after Uma but before Kofi.

Who finished fourth?
questions.explanation: Nadia, Pia and Uma come in that order. Lou is after Uma and before Kofi, and since Kofi is directly after Rhys, Lou must also be before Rhys. The order is Nadia, Pia, Uma, Lou, Rhys, Kofi.

questions.stem:
Hana: Students in the school choir get better marks in music than other students. So joining the choir must improve your music marks.

Which one of the following shows the mistake Hana has made?
options: Some choir students do not get the top mark in music.
Students who join may already have been good at music.
Choir practice takes time away from other school subjects.
Hana has not said how many students are in the choir.
questions.explanation: The choir and the good marks go together, but the good musicians may have joined because they were already good. Hana assumes the choir causes the marks. A few choir students missing top marks does not affect her claim about averages.

questions.stem:
A lost hat is in one of three lockers. Each locker has a note on it, and exactly one note is true.

Locker 1: "The hat is in this locker."
Locker 2: "The hat is not in this locker."
Locker 3: "The hat is not in locker 1."

Which locker is the hat in?
questions.explanation: If the hat is in locker 1, notes 1 and 2 are both true. If it is in locker 3, notes 2 and 3 are both true. Only locker 2 makes exactly one note (note 3) true.

questions.stem:
Oscar: The new bus timetable has the bus arriving at my stop at 8:10 instead of 8:20. That means I will get to school ten minutes earlier from now on.

Which assumption has Oscar made?
options: Arriving at school ten minutes earlier is a good thing.
The bus was often late under the old timetable.
The trip to school will take no longer than before.
Other students from his street will catch the earlier bus too.
questions.explanation: Leaving ten minutes earlier only means arriving ten minutes earlier if the trip is no longer than before. Oscar does not say whether arriving early is good, so that is not something he assumed.

questions.stem: Rosa uses each of the digits 2, 5, 7 and 9 once to make two 2-digit numbers. She adds the two numbers. What is the smallest total she can make?
questions.explanation: To keep the total small, put the smallest digits, 2 and 5, in the tens places: 27 + 59 = 86 (29 + 57 also gives 86). Making 25 + 79 gives 104.

questions.stem:
At the swimming carnival, every student who swam in the relay also swam freestyle. No student who swam backstroke swam freestyle. Some students who swam backstroke also swam breaststroke.

If the information is true, which one of these statements must also be true?
options: Some students who swam breaststroke swam in the relay.
Every student who swam freestyle swam in the relay.
No student who swam breaststroke swam freestyle.
No student who swam in the relay swam backstroke.
questions.explanation: Relay swimmers all swam freestyle, and freestyle swimmers never swam backstroke, so no relay swimmer swam backstroke. Breaststroke swimmers who did not swim backstroke might still have swum freestyle, so that option need not be true.

questions.stem: A clock gains 3 minutes every hour. It is set to the correct time at 9:00 am. Later the same day, the clock shows 3:18 pm. What is the correct time?
questions.explanation: Each real hour, the clock moves forward 63 minutes. From 9:00 am to 3:18 pm the clock has moved 378 minutes, which is 6 lots of 63, so 6 real hours have passed and the time is 3:00 pm.

questions.stem:
In a quiz of 12 questions, each correct answer earns 3 points, each wrong answer loses 1 point and a question left blank scores 0. Farah scored 18 points.

Theo says: "Farah must have got 7 answers right."
Anika says: "Farah must have answered every question."

If the information is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.explanation: Farah could have got 6 right, 0 wrong and 6 blank (18 points) or 7 right, 3 wrong and 2 blank (21 minus 3 is 18). Either way some questions were blank, and she need not have got 7 right, so neither is correct.

questions.stem: A bag holds 5 red, 4 blue and 3 green counters. Without looking, Jai takes counters out one at a time. What is the fewest counters he must take out to be sure he has at least one of each colour?
questions.explanation: In the unluckiest case he takes all 5 red and all 4 blue first, which is 9 counters with no green. The next one must be green, so he needs 10 to be sure.

questions.stem: Sami says "I know," although "he hadn't known". Why does he say this?
options: He had already fixed the tail himself
He hopes Mr Okafor will help
He is trying to be polite
He doesn't want to look foolish
questions.explanation: He has just failed in front of someone, and that night he rebuilds the kite "alone, with the door shut", which shows his pride. A polite reply would not need to be untrue, and he does not accept help until much later.

questions.stem: Why does the writer include the detail that a magpie "inspected it with obvious disgust"?
options: to add humour to the failure
to show the oval is dangerous
to hint that rain is coming
to make us pity the magpie
questions.explanation: Giving the magpie a human reaction of "disgust" makes the crashed kite funny rather than sad. The magpie does nothing threatening, so it does not show danger.

questions.stem: The words "as far as Sami could tell" suggest that
options: Mr Okafor hides his tomato cages
Sami watches Mr Okafor closely every day
Sami may have misjudged Mr Okafor
questions.explanation: The phrase limits the claim that Mr Okafor builds "nothing at all" to Sami's view, hinting that he knows more than Sami thinks, which the shed scenes later prove. He is still gardening; he returns "to his tomatoes" at the end.

questions.stem: Which words best describe the way Mr Okafor teaches Sami?
questions.explanation: He "asked questions instead of giving answers" and nodded at wrong answers "as if a wrong answer were a useful thing to have found". He never rushes or scolds Sami, so "strict and impatient" is the opposite.

questions.stem: The kite climbs "until it was a red fleck against the blue". A "fleck" is
questions.explanation: The kite is "so high he had to tip his head right back", so from the ground it looks like a tiny spot of colour. It is flying well, not torn.

questions.stem: Which statement best sums up the extract?
options: A boy beats his rival by cheating
An engineer builds a boy's kite
Kite Day is ruined by bad weather
questions.explanation: Sami fails twice alone, then passes the kite over the fence, works with Mr Okafor and succeeds. Mr Okafor asks questions while Sami does the work, so he does not simply build it for him.

questions.stem: The simile "cold as a dinner plate" helps the reader to
options: imagine a meal on the beach
picture an everyday kind of cold
see how white the sand is
hear the sand crunch under their feet
questions.explanation: Most readers know the cool, hard feel of a plate, so the comparison makes the cold sand easy to imagine. The poem is about temperature here, not the colour or sound of the sand.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the short sentences "They do not race. They do not rush."?
options: They show the swimmers are exhausted
They hint that a race will start
They make the swimmers seem angry
They stress the swimmers' calm pace
questions.explanation: The short, even sentences match the steady swimming described next: "slow, then slower, end to end". Nothing suggests tiredness; the swimmers are "laughing".

questions.stem: By the end of the poem, which word best describes the speaker's attitude towards the swimmers?
questions.explanation: The speaker watches closely and finally imagines the swimmers as once "nervous" and "young like me", showing respect for their courage. The opening line, "Nobody sensible swims in June", sounds scornful, but the poem moves away from that view.

questions.stem: What does the line "as if the cold were no more than skin" suggest?
options: The cold has hurt their skin
The cold does not trouble them
They are too cold to keep going
questions.explanation: Treating the cold as only skin-deep means it does not reach or bother them, which fits their slow, relaxed swimming. They keep swimming "end to end", so they are not about to stop.

questions.stem: What does the speaker realise in the final stanza?
options: The sea is too rough for swimming
Only older people swim in winter
They will never be brave enough
questions.explanation: The speaker thinks the swimmers "must have been / nervous once, and young like me", so their confidence was learned. This makes the speaker's own first swim seem possible, not impossible.

questions.stem: Why does the writer describe ghost nets as "hunters" with "no eyes, no brain and no hunger"?
options: They kill though no one uses them
They move quickly through the water
questions.explanation: The next sentences explain that the nets "keep catching animals long after anyone is fishing with them": they kill without purpose. "No brain" makes clear they are not actually alive.

questions.stem: Which of these ideas from the article is an opinion rather than a fact?
options: Many nets drift here from nearby seas
Rangers haul the nets above the high-tide line
The rangers' work deserves more recognition
Net sculptures are shown in galleries
questions.explanation: Whether work "deserves far more recognition" is the writer's judgement. Where nets come from, what rangers do and where sculptures have been shown can all be checked.

questions.stem: Why do rangers drag nets above the high-tide line?
options: so artists can collect them easily
so that scientists can measure the mesh
so turtles can rest in the shade
so the sea cannot carry them off again
questions.explanation: The article says they haul nets up "so that they cannot wash back out to sea". Artists do reuse some nets, but that is not the reason given for moving them.

questions.stem: Which detail supports the claim that "Australia cannot solve the problem alone"?
options: Most nets come from foreign boats
The nets can be very long
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains that "most of them do not come from Australian boats" but drift from neighbouring seas, so other countries must help. The size of the nets shows the danger, not who is responsible.

questions.stem: Which best describes how the article is organised?
options: events in the order they happened
a problem, then efforts to tackle it
two sides of a debate weighed up
one turtle's life from birth to death
questions.explanation: It first explains what ghost nets are and the harm they do, then where they come from, then the work of rangers and artists, and ends with what could fix it. It does not follow dates, and no opposing side is argued.

questions.stem: Ghost nets are not only a problem in the north. [[1]], fishing gear is one of the most common kinds of plastic rubbish found on Australian beaches. [[2]] nets are made of strong plastic, they can last for hundreds of years in the sea. This is why clean-up crews try to remove them [[3]] they break into small pieces that are almost impossible to collect.
questions.explanation: "Across the country" widens the problem beyond the north; nothing is being contrasted or caused. "Because" gives the reason the nets last so long. Crews must act "before" the nets break up, since the small pieces are "almost impossible to collect".

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 1?
options: In some northern areas, termites ate through the wooden poles until they fell.
Many people wanted a faster way to connect the colonies with the rest of the world.
To boost it, repeater stations were built about 250 kilometres apart.
Its two ends were joined at Frew's Ponds, near the middle of the continent.
Today, most long-distance messages travel through cables made of glass fibre.
questions.explanation: The paragraph describes a problem (slow news) and the next sentence begins "The solution was", so the gap must express the wish for something faster. The glass fibre sentence jumps to the present day and breaks the story.

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 2?
options: Many people wanted a faster way to connect the colonies with the rest of the world.
In some northern areas, termites ate through the wooden poles until they fell.
To boost it, repeater stations were built about 250 kilometres apart.
Today, most long-distance messages travel through cables made of glass fibre.
From there, a wire would run south through the centre to Adelaide.
questions.explanation: "From there" refers back to Darwin, and the next sentence, "This meant building a line about 3,200 kilometres long", needs a route to describe. The termite sentence belongs to the paragraph about poles, after work has started.

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 3?
options: Heat was not the only problem.
Many people wanted a faster way to connect the colonies with the rest of the world.
In some northern areas, termites ate through the wooden poles until they fell.
To boost it, repeater stations were built about 250 kilometres apart.
Today, most long-distance messages travel through cables made of glass fibre.
questions.explanation: The paragraph has just mentioned temperatures "above 40 degrees" and the next sentence adds floods, so "Heat was not the only problem" links the two. The termite sentence would leave the following words "Another enemy was much smaller" with nothing to compare.

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 4?
options: Many people wanted a faster way to connect the colonies with the rest of the world.
From there, a wire would run south through the centre to Adelaide.
Its two ends were joined at Frew's Ponds, near the middle of the continent.
In some northern areas, termites ate through the wooden poles until they fell.
Today, most long-distance messages travel through cables made of glass fibre.
questions.explanation: "Another enemy was much smaller" is answered by termites, and "In those areas" needs a place to refer to: "some northern areas". Iron poles replacing wooden ones only makes sense after wood has been eaten.

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 5?
options: Many people wanted a faster way to connect the colonies with the rest of the world.
In some northern areas, termites ate through the wooden poles until they fell.
To boost it, repeater stations were built about 250 kilometres apart.
Its two ends were joined at Frew's Ponds, near the middle of the continent.
Today, most long-distance messages travel through cables made of glass fibre.
questions.explanation: "At each one" needs a plural place to point back to: the repeater stations. "To boost it" also answers the problem that the signal "grew weaker".

questions.stem: Which sentence best fills Gap 6?
options: Its two ends were joined at Frew's Ponds, near the middle of the continent.
Many people wanted a faster way to connect the colonies with the rest of the world.
From there, a wire would run south through the centre to Adelaide.
To boost it, repeater stations were built about 250 kilometres apart.
Today, most long-distance messages travel through cables made of glass fibre.
questions.explanation: "Its two ends" refers to the line that "was completed", and joining them is what made the whole connection work. The glass fibre sentence fits the topic but leaps to today, which clashes with "For the first time" in the next sentence.

questions.stem: In which extract does the writer ask questions of the person they are writing to?
questions.explanation: Tilly asks Jess "Did you make the netball team?" and about Mr Fraser. Extract C mentions wondering what an arvo was, but it does not put a question to the reader.

questions.stem: Which extract describes a journey that is repeated every year?
questions.explanation: The moths fly to the Alps "each spring" and their young "repeat the trip". The families in Extracts A and C move once.
